fields.page_status: ok = summary from page; otherwise no summary

links.author: Martin Underhill (tempertemper)
key_points: Users naturally resist interface changes regardless of benefit
Existing user bases lack disabled people due to historical exclusion
Unanimous negative feedback doesn't mean the change is worse
Roll changes out incrementally to minimize disruption
my_comments: Feedback from existing users likely to be negative because not including accessibility from the start
links.summary: Explores the tension between user feedback and accessibility improvements in organizations that historically lacked inclusive design. Explains why existing users often resist accessible changes and how a homogenous user base can mask the needs of disabled people who were previously excluded.
links.title: User 'wants' versus accessibility

links.author: Chris Coyier (Frontend Masters)
key_points: Modal dialogs trap focus and add a backdrop
Popovers can be controlled with HTML only (popovertarget)
Dialogs move focus inside; popovers leave it on the trigger
Popovers light-dismiss on outside click unless manual
links.summary: Compares the HTML <dialog> element with the popover attribute. Both are hidden by default and render in the top layer, but they differ in focus management, how they're controlled and when to use them: dialogs suit modal interactions with focus trapping, popovers offer HTML-only controls and light dismiss.
links.title: What's the Difference Between HTML's Dialog Element and Popovers?

links.author: HuffPost Contributor
key_points: Invisible disabilities can require wheelchair use without paralysis
Parking placards cover many conditions beyond mobility
Identity-first language is a legitimate preference
my_comments: Myths about disability
links.summary: Debunks common misconceptions about disabled people: wheelchair users may be able to walk, accessible parking placards cover non-visible conditions, identity-first language is valid, and disabled people want respect rather than 'inspiration porn'.
links.title: Basic Myths about Disability I Can't Believe We Still Have to Debunk

links.author: Devon Persing
key_points: Combines social-science foundations with actionable program strategy
Addresses systemic burnout among accessibility professionals
DRM-free ebook; also available via libraries (OverDrive)
my_comments: Accessibility Operations Guidebook
links.summary: Announces the Accessibility Operations Guidebook ebook, which addresses burnout in accessibility work with organizational-psychology theory and practical strategies for building sustainable, data-driven accessibility programs that center disabled people.
links.title: The Accessibility Operations Guidebook is out

links.author: Jo Chang (Bootcamp, Medium)
key_points: Access8Math adds math reading and navigation modes
Web editor for teachers, no Nemeth expertise needed
my_comments: Math on NVDA
links.status_note: Original scribe.rip mirror link is broken; use the Medium URL
links.summary: Looks at Access8Math, a free NVDA add-on from the Taiwanese nonprofit Coseeing, which addresses barriers blind students face learning math digitally. Covers NVDA's weak MathML support, Access8Math's reading/interaction modes, and a web editor that lets teachers create accessible math without knowing Nemeth Braille.
links.title: Designing for accessibility: enhancing math learning for the blind using the NVDA screen reader

links.author: Equalize Digital and WP Buffs
key_points: Covers accessibility laws and legal risk
When to fix in-house vs. hire help
my_comments: Small business playbook
links.summary: Free 44-page ebook helping small businesses understand and implement website accessibility on WordPress: laws and compliance, testing tools and methods, remediation, and recommended accessible themes and plugins.
links.title: The Small Business Accessibility Playbook for WordPress

links.author: beeps (GOV.UK Design System team)
key_points: Escape cancels page loading in browsers
Escape doesn't count as user activation, so it can't trigger the redirect
Escape is heavily used by OSes and assistive tech
Shift chosen as least problematic alternative
my_comments: Use of escape key
links.summary: Explains why GOV.UK's Exit this Page safety component (for people at risk of domestic abuse) uses repeated Shift presses instead of Escape, covering browser behavior, transient-activation rules and assistive technology conflicts.
links.title: Why GOV.UK's Exit this Page component doesn't use the Escape key

links.author: Steve Faulkner
key_points: Alt text depends on the image's purpose and context
Charts need data-based descriptions; use figure/figcaption or links for long ones
my_comments: Thorough alt text advice
links.summary: Comprehensive alt text guidance originally written for the HTML5 spec (2010-2014), covering about 19 image scenarios with examples and code: decorative images, icon buttons, charts, images of text, and long descriptions.
links.title: Old alt text advice

links.author: Patrick Sturdivant (Deque)
key_points: EU rules may exempt aircraft entertainment systems
United Airlines leads on accessible IFE and Braille
my_comments: Experience of blind person traveling (there’s also a part 1 and 2, which are also great)
links.summary: A blind traveler's account of his return flight from Germany to Texas, covering Frankfurt airport and business-class travel, and proposing improvements for airlines such as Braille cabin labeling, accessible in-flight entertainment and clearer seat-belt alerts.
links.title: Patrick's European vacation: traveling internationally as a person with a disability (Part Three)

links.author: TPGi (now Vispero)
my_comments: In-depth article about label positioning with form control
links.status_note: TPGi blog moved to Vispero; the new page couldn't be read automatically
links.title: Assume the Position: A Labeling Story

links.author: Jonathan Hassell (Hassell Inclusion)
key_points: Testing finds problems; fixing needs organizational commitment
AIPM weighs affected audience, impact and cost
my_comments: AIPM - matrix for determining who to prioritize AX fixes
links.summary: Argues accessibility testing is pointless without remediation, citing widespread failures after the UK 2020 public-sector accessibility deadline. Introduces the Accessibility Issue Prioritisation Matrix (AIPM) to prioritize fixes by audience affected, severity of impact and cost to fix.
links.title: The goal of accessibility isn't to find issues, it's to fix them

links.author: Domingos de Oliveira (netz-barrierefrei.de)
my_comments: What AX testing can and can’t do
links.title: What automated accessibility testing can and can't do

links.author: Google (Android Accessibility Help)
my_comments: What’s new with Talkback
links.summary: Release notes for TalkBack 15.0, Android's screen reader: generative-AI image descriptions (server-side or on-device on Pixel 9), punctuation verbosity controls, 'Read from next' renamed 'Read from focused item', and new Braille selection gestures.
links.title: What's new with TalkBack 15.0

links.author: Dani Devesa Derksen-Staats (Accessibility up to 11)
key_points: Unlabeled icon buttons are a frequent miss
Custom components need explicit accessibility setup
Support the largest Dynamic Type sizes
my_comments: A bunch of iOS AX tips with links to other resources
links.summary: A 24-day series on common iOS accessibility issues and fixes for UIKit and SwiftUI: unlabeled elements, header traits, images, buttons, grouping, toggles, modals, contrast, touch targets, Dynamic Type and Reduce Motion, with links to further resources.
links.title: Advent of iOS Accessibility

links.author: Bas Thomas (Bas Broek)
key_points: VoiceOver support is a foundation for Voice Control
Combining elements helps VoiceOver but can break Voice Control
Voice Control lacks affordances for secondary/'ghost' actions
my_comments: Bas’ Blog - a lot on iOS AX tips
links.summary: Documents building an iOS survey component and the conflicting requirements of VoiceOver and Voice Control: combining elements helps VoiceOver but can hide actions from Voice Control. Settles on a balanced compromise and calls for better Voice Control documentation.
links.title: Optimizing for VoiceOver and Voice Control

links.author: Tj Squires (TPGi / Vispero)
key_points: Check client privacy before using AI
Compare AI descriptions with alt text
AI can hallucinate; can't judge contrast
my_comments: How blind engineer is using AI to test accessibility of photos
links.summary: A blind accessibility engineer describes using generative AI (JAWS PictureSmart) in testing: analyzing screenshots, comparing visual vs. programmatic information, and checking alt text, while stressing client privacy and verifying AI output.
links.title: Putting AI to the (Accessibility) Test

links.author: Florian Schroiff (The A11Y Collective)
key_points: Live regions announce updates without moving focus
Choose polite vs assertive by urgency
Test in NVDA, JAWS and VoiceOver
my_comments: Aria-live
links.summary: Guide to using ARIA live regions to announce dynamic content to screen reader users: aria-live values off/polite/assertive, aria-atomic and aria-relevant, code examples, common mistakes and testing across screen readers.
links.title: The Complete Guide to ARIA Live Regions for Developers

links.author: Ashlee M Boyer
key_points: AI personas can't authentically tell disabled people's stories
Automated tools catch only about 13-40% of issues
my_comments: Mentions that testing at most can find 40% of issues
links.summary: Critiques an 'a11y-AI' tool that uses AI-generated disabled personas, arguing synthetic characters can't represent disabled people's experiences or replace human expertise, and that accessibility problems stem from ableism, not lack of awareness.
links.title: How to Dehumanize Accessibility with AI

links.author: Meryl Evans (Equal Entry)
my_comments: Equal Entry - I like their legal discussions in general
links.summary: Describes the burdensome FCC captioning complaint process under the CVAA, using the author's report about ION TV censoring profanity in captions but not audio. Argues the process demands too much from disabled consumers and lacks follow-up to confirm fixes.
links.title: Headaches with FCC Reporting on Captioning Problems Per CVAA

links.author: Carme Mias
key_points: Top failures: contrast, alt text, form labels, empty links/buttons
About 25% of the UK population reports a disability
Developers are the last link in the chain
my_comments: Gives details about top AX issues
links.summary: Uses WebAIM Million data (95.9% of top homepages have detectable errors, about 56 per page) to argue that the most common failures (low contrast, missing alt text, unlabeled forms) are easy to fix, and that developers must take ownership.
links.title: Why are we so rubbish at accessibility?

links.author: Andrew Downie (OZeWAI)
key_points: Skip links satisfy WCAG 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks
Hidden skip links are a problem for sighted keyboard users
Consider several skip links on long pages
my_comments: In-depth discussion about skip links for keyboard-only users
Gets me thinking why regions aren’t expected to be focusable
links.summary: Argues skip links should be visible rather than hidden until focus, since keyboard-only users benefit most from them, while screen reader users have other navigation methods. Recommends multiple skip links on long pages.
links.title: Don't Hide Skip Links

links.author: The A11Y Collective
key_points: Tools like Seeing AI and Lookout help but aren't infallible
Speech recognition struggles with accents and noise
Include disabled people throughout, not just at the end
my_comments: Discusses considerations when using AI for accessibility
links.summary: Examines how AI can help accessibility (image description, speech recognition, adaptive interfaces) while addressing limitations: errors, accent and noise problems, automated 'fixes' that interfere with assistive tech, privacy and training-data bias. Stresses involving disabled people throughout development.
links.title: AI and Accessibility: Ethical Considerations and Solutions

links.author: Kyle Wiggers (TechCrunch)
key_points: NFB called its marketing disrespectful and misleading
my_comments: Interesting that only 1 company was targeted
links.summary: The FTC fined overlay vendor accessiBe $1 million for falsely claiming its AI plug-in makes sites WCAG/ADA compliant and for presenting sponsored reviews as independent. The order bars overstating capabilities and requires endorsement disclosures.
links.title: FTC orders AI accessibility startup accessiBe to pay $1M for misleading advertising

links.author: Steve Faulkner
key_points: Non-generic child elements fragment link announcements
Use span or role=none as a workaround
my_comments: Issue with links on VO in iOS
links.summary: Documents an iOS VoiceOver/WebKit bug where links containing non-generic HTML elements are announced and counted as multiple links. Workaround: use generic elements (span) or role="none"; a WebKit bug was filed.
links.title: super short note on links in iOS with VoiceOver

links.author: Natalie Stormann (Slack Engineering)
key_points: Check only after full render to avoid false positives
my_comments: Slack using AXE testing
links.summary: How Slack added Axe checks to its Playwright end-to-end tests to complement manual testing toward WCAG 2.1: why they moved off Jest/RTL, excluding known issues, filtering to critical violations, running checks after full render, and a Jira triage workflow.
links.title: Automated Accessibility Testing at Slack

links.author: Whitney Lewis (Pope Tech)
key_points: Manual: slower but judges real impact and AT compatibility
Monthly scans + annual manual sample testing
my_comments: Automated and manual testing working together
links.summary: Explains the strengths and limits of automated vs. manual accessibility testing and how combining them gives breadth and depth. Suggests a realistic strategy: monthly automated scans, annual manual testing of sample pages, and testing changes before release.
links.title: Automated and manual accessibility testing work best together

links.author: Salma Alam-Naylor (whitep4nth3r)
key_points: Learn Talon's alphabet with deliberate practice
Expect a learning curve; combine tools
my_comments: Account of how a software engineer codes with voice
links.summary: A developer with severe hand pain describes learning to code by voice with Talon and Cursorless, what didn't work, and practical advice for others.
links.title: How I learned to code with my voice

links.author: Karl Groves and 1,000+ signatories
key_points: Automated repairs fail for images, forms, keyboard, dynamic content
my_comments: Issues with overlays
Article describing lawsuits with overlays: https://www.lflegal.com/2025/02/userway-overlay-lawsuit/

related.author: Lainey Feingold (Law Office of Lainey Feingold)
related.summary: A small online florist (BloomsyBox) filed a class action against overlay vendor UserWay after being sued by a blind user despite paying for the overlay; alleges false claims of lawsuit protection. Notes over 1,000 2024 ADA suits against sites using overlays.
related.title: Another Web Access Overlay Company Sued by a Small Business

links.summary: Open letter signed by 1,000+ accessibility professionals explaining why accessibility overlays can't make sites compliant, can worsen the experience for disabled users, raise privacy concerns and use deceptive marketing. Includes testimony from disabled users.
links.title: Overlay Fact Sheet

links.author: Christian 'Schepp' Schaefer
key_points: Find-in-page is a real navigation strategy
Chromium-only support at time of writing
my_comments: Find-in-page accessibility
Hidden=”until-found”
links.summary: Notes that some blind users navigate primarily with the browser's find-in-page, and proposes hidden="until-found" so visually hidden labels (e.g., on icon-only buttons) can still be found by search.
links.title: Rethinking Find-in-Page Accessibility: Making Hidden Text Work for Everyone

links.author: Martin Underhill (tempertemper)
key_points: W3C example needs 70+ lines of JS
Arrow-key behavior conflicts with Tab expectations
Most sites never need a menubar
my_comments: Questioning menubar W3C example
links.summary: Argues against using the ARIA menubar pattern for website navigation: menubars are for application actions, while site navigation should be simple lists of links. The menubar's arrow-key model confuses keyboard and screen reader users.
links.title: There's no such thing as 'menubar navigation'

links.author: Nat Tarnoff
my_comments: Nice article about input
links.summary: Explains WCAG 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose: native labels, correct input types and autocomplete attributes, and how autocomplete supports independence, password managers and security.
links.title: A11y 101: 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose

links.author: Caitlin de Rooij (The A11Y Collective)
key_points: Many more people than the ~13% with cognitive disabilities benefit
Reduce overload, manage focus, allow time
Plain language, consistent navigation, clear errors
Test with people who have cognitive disabilities
my_comments: Nice overview of how to make web/mobile products accessible for people with cognitive disabilities
links.summary: Guide to cognitive accessibility: how cognitive disabilities affect web use, relevant WCAG 2.2 criteria, design patterns (plain language, consistent navigation, forgiving forms, memory aids) and testing with real users.
links.title: Best Practices for Cognitive Accessibility in Web Design

links.author: Dave Davies
key_points: Ratio measures luminance difference, not hue
~1 in 12 men have colour vision deficiency
my_comments: Nice in-depth discussion in text color-contrast, esp motivation behind 4.5:1 rule
links.summary: Explains the science behind WCAG's 4.5:1 contrast ratio: relative luminance (brightness, not hue), how red/green/blue are weighted, colour vision deficiency, and how the standard evolved from a 3:1 baseline adjusted for reduced vision. Includes practical tools.
links.title: WCAG Colour Contrast: What does the 4.5:1 ratio actually mean?

links.author: Michelle Neysa (AccessTime)
key_points: Test across orientations; use adaptive layouts
Benefits users with mounted devices and motor/visual needs
my_comments: Android 16 won’t allow locking in portrait and landscape mode
links.summary: Android 16 removes apps' ability to lock orientation and resizability on large screens, forcing adaptive layouts. That helps foldables and people who depend on landscape mode (e.g., mounted devices, motor or vision needs), aligning with WCAG 1.3.4 Orientation.
links.title: Android 16's Transition to Adaptive Apps: A Major Victory for Accessibility

links.author: The A11Y Collective
key_points: Links an element to descriptive text by ID
Pitfalls: overuse, broken IDs, repeating the label
Prefer native HTML; visible descriptions help everyone
my_comments: Aria-describedby
links.summary: How to use aria-describedby to link elements to supplementary descriptive text for screen reader users, with examples for forms, buttons and dialogs, common mistakes, and testing advice.
links.title: Implementing aria-describedby for Web Accessibility

links.author: Joe Dolson
key_points: Critique exposes needed effort, not blame
my_comments: Like his statement that accessibility has to be done with intention
links.summary: Reflections after the CSUN Assistive Technology Conference on how shared struggles build community, WordPress 6.8's ~95 accessibility improvements, and why publicly critiquing site accessibility (on The Accessibility Show) is about showing the intentional work required.
links.title: Because we're not alone (reflections on CSUN)

links.author: Abra
my_comments: Mobile ax courses
links.summary: E-learning platform for mobile app accessibility with a free 45-minute kickoff course and paid courses on testing, common issues and platform-specific iOS/Android training, with certificates. Instructors are involved in the W3C Mobile Accessibility Task Force.
links.title: Abra Academy: learn how to make your apps accessible

links.author: Access Armada
key_points: Use semantic HTML, not div soup
Use Fragments to avoid excess nesting
my_comments: Common ax issues when using React
links.summary: Argues the real question is whether React makes accessible apps easier or harder. Common React problems: div soup, weak semantics, ARIA misuse, SPA route-change focus management and client-side rendering performance.
links.title: Is React Accessible? That's the Wrong Question

links.author: Anne-Mieke Bovelett
key_points: Beauty and accessibility aren't in conflict
my_comments: Github experience
links.summary: Uses GitHub's redesigned, animated signup flow, which respects reduced-motion preferences, as proof that accessible design and visual beauty can coexist.
links.title: Designers, your excuse is gone. Stunning, animated and accessible. Yes, you can!

links.author: Access Aces
key_points: AT detection discloses disability without consent
Overlays can track users across sites
my_comments: Privacy for disabled people on apps
Interesting argument for why shouldn’t track if someone is using a screen reader
links.summary: A blind author argues that detecting assistive technology violates privacy by forcing disability disclosure, and that separate 'accessible' versions, remote sighted-assistance apps, overlays and connected devices trade disabled people's data for access.
links.title: What disabled people have to give up in the name of accessibility (privacy rights of people with disabilities)

links.author: Eevis Panula
key_points: AI repeats inaccessible patterns from training data
Redundant contentDescription hurts screen reader users
focusable() + clickable() creates duplicate tab stops
my_comments: Nice demonstration explaining why certain innocuous AX code causes problems in Android
links.summary: Tests Google's Gemini generating a Jetpack Compose Android app in two iterations. The first had major issues (redundant contentDescriptions, missing scroll, extra focus stops); the second was better, for unclear reasons. Tested with TalkBack, Switch Access and more.
links.title: Does Gemini Generate Accessible Android Apps?

links.author: Akash Shukla (TPGi / Vispero)
key_points: Name should match or start with visible label
iOS 18+ Voice Control accepts names that begin with the label
my_comments: End of article keeps tips on what to do if visible and ax label can’t match
links.summary: Explains WCAG 2.5.3 Label in Name: a control's accessible name must contain its visible label so speech-input users can say what they see. Covers common failures (missing names, mismatched text, extra interspersed words, reordering) and best practice of identical or label-first names.
links.title: How to meet SC 2.5.3 Label in Name

links.author: Blake Watson
key_points: Persistent portfolio-building led to a job
my_comments: Person with spinal muscular atrophy describes their path to employment
links.summary: A web developer with spinal muscular atrophy reflects on ten years of employment after six years unemployed, his path into web design, remote work, and how means-tested, state-by-state disability programs discourage employment.
links.title: A Decade of Employment

links.author: Alicia Evans (TPGi / Vispero)
my_comments: Discussion of required for groups
I like how in-depth this article is, author clearly has extensive AX experience
links.summary: How to communicate that a group of radio buttons or checkboxes is required: use fieldset/legend, note aria-required doesn't work on fieldset, put the asterisk on the group label, add 'required' text to the legend, and state rules like 'pick at least one' for checkboxes.
links.title: Everything's More Complicated in Groups: Required Groups

links.author: Adrian Roselli
my_comments: Request to Google for releases and accessibility
links.summary: Criticizes Google for repeatedly shipping web-platform features with accessibility barriers (e.g., toasts, CSS carousels) and sidelining accessibility experts and disabled users; asks that features meet WCAG AA before release.
links.title: My Request to Google on Accessibility

links.author: W3C Mobile Accessibility Task Force
key_points: Covers all WCAG 2.2 A/AA criteria for mobile
my_comments: Draft of Mobile WCAG standards
links.summary: W3C draft note on applying WCAG 2.2 A and AA success criteria to native, mobile web and hybrid apps, replacing web terms (e.g., 'web page') with mobile concepts like screens and views. Informative, not normative.
links.title: Guidance on Applying WCAG 2.2 to Mobile Applications (WCAG2Mobile)

links.author: Apple Newsroom
key_points: Accessibility Nutrition Labels in the App Store
my_comments: New Apple AX features
links.summary: Apple's 2025 accessibility announcements: App Store Accessibility Nutrition Labels, Magnifier for Mac, Braille Access, Accessibility Reader, Live Captions on Apple Watch, Vision Pro zoom and Live Recognition, and Switch Control for brain-computer interfaces.
links.title: Apple unveils powerful accessibility features coming later this year

links.author: Torque, Inc.
my_comments: Website of accessible sites, can filter by WCAG level
links.summary: A curated gallery of well-designed websites selected for accessibility, filterable by WCAG level (A/AA/AAA), site type, industry and colour.
links.title: AAA11Y: Accessible Website Gallery

links.author: Adrian Roselli
key_points: Short messages: focus close button can be fine
Long/complex content: focus the dialog or heading
Screen readers announce dialog role inconsistently
my_comments: Focus in dialogs
links.summary: Rejects a single rule for initial focus in modal dialogs: it depends on content type (simple message, interactive, action-required, form), length, and the risk of accidental actions. Includes screen reader testing showing inconsistent dialog-role announcements.
links.title: Where to Put Focus When Opening a Modal Dialog

links.author: Equal Entry
key_points: AI augments, not replaces, accessibility expertise
Combine linting with AI to limit hallucination
my_comments: Accessibility Nerd

links.title: From Curiosity to Creation: The Story Behind Accessibility Nerd

links.author: The A11Y Collective
my_comments: Mentions course for IAAP
links.summary: How to make web infographics accessible: simple design, text transcripts and alt text, 4.5:1 contrast and not relying on colour, controllable animation, semantic HTML/SVG rather than flat images, and testing.
links.title: Implement WCAG Rules in Your Infographics

links.author: International Association of Accessibility Professionals (IAAP)
my_comments: CPACC CEAC opportunities

links.title: Robust roles on Android

links.author: Jason Taylor (UsableNet)
my_comments: Mid-year Lawsuit report for 2025
links.summary: Over 2,000 digital accessibility lawsuits were filed in the first half of 2025, with a projected ~20% rise for the year. Filings are shifting to state courts (especially New York), e-commerce is the top target, and accessibility widgets still offer no legal protection.
links.title: 2025 Midyear Accessibility Lawsuit Report: Key Legal Trends

links.author: Léonie Watson (TetraLogical)
key_points: Technically accessible sites can still lack needed product info
Agents act for users via conversation
Open questions on content consistency and legal duty
my_comments: Accessibility and agentic web
links.summary: Considers how agentic AI (e.g., conversational shopping agents) could help disabled people get things done without navigating websites, while raising concerns about inconsistent content, falling web traffic and unclear legal obligations.
links.title: Accessibility and the agentic web

links.author: Hidde de Vries
key_points: Context breaks things (e.g., hidden focus indicators)
Design systems should document what's been tested
my_comments: Components and accessibility
links.summary: WCAG conformance applies only to full pages, not components, because accessibility depends on customization, combination and context. Components should be built and documented for accessibility, but real conformance is assessed on the finished experience.
links.title: Can components conform to WCAG?

links.author: Craig Abbott
my_comments: Nice article about tension with WCAG compliance and being accessible
links.summary: Argues that labeling audit findings 'best practice' makes real barriers sound optional, is inconsistent between practitioners and can sound arrogant. Suggests 'standard of care' or just 'accessibility issues' instead.
links.title: "Best practice" is just your opinion

links.author: Google Chrome Developers
my_comments: Chrome AX reference
links.summary: Reference for Chrome DevTools accessibility features: Lighthouse audits, the Accessibility pane and accessibility tree, ARIA inspection, emulating vision deficiencies and media preferences, reflow testing and finding low-contrast text.
links.title: Accessibility features reference (Chrome DevTools)

links.author: Open UI Community Group (W3C)
my_comments: W3C community effort to improve UI components
links.summary: W3C community group working to let developers style and extend built-in UI controls (select, checkbox, date pickers) by specifying their parts, states, behaviors and accessibility requirements, with research on 30+ components.

links.author: Ars Technica
my_comments: Neurodivergent benefiting from AI
links.title: Study finds neurodiverse workers more satisfied with AI assistants

links.author: Craig Abbott

my_comments: Argument not to use AI for screen reader users

links.author: Shawn Lawton Henry (W3C WAI)
my_comments: W3C Mobile AX standards
links.summary: Explains that W3C covers mobile accessibility through existing standards (WCAG, UAAG, ATAG, WAI-ARIA) rather than separate mobile guidelines, and points to WCAG2Mobile guidance and the Mobile Accessibility Task Force.

links.author: Appt (guest: Daniel Devesa Derksen-Staats)

links.summary: Newsletter issue with iOS accessibility takeaways from SwiftLeeds (developers underestimate issues; native components help) plus recent iOS and Android resources on custom controls, keyboard access and focus management.
links.title: Appt Mobile Accessibility News, Issue #75

links.author: Diogo Melo (Axess Lab)
key_points: Default VoiceOver order didn't match the domain
accessibilitySortPriority changes order without changing layout

links.author: Access * Ability newsletter

links.author: Mike Gower (IBM Design)

Too many feedback buttons add noise
Floating launchers create hard-to-reach tab stops

links.author: Deeksha Yadav (TPGi / Vispero)

links.author: Abra
key_points: One AT at a time, screen by screen
my_comments: Thorough article about how to test for accessibility

links.title: Practical guide to mobile accessibility testing

links.author: Diogo Melo (Axess Lab)
key_points: Semantics fix multiple assistive technologies at once
The .isButton trait is recognized by VO, FKA and Voice Control
my_comments: Nice demonstration of how button traits drastically improve UI
links.summary: Starts from a deliberately inaccessible SwiftUI app and shows that two fixes, grouping elements and adding the .isButton trait, made it work with VoiceOver, Full Keyboard Access and Voice Control.
links.title: How Button Traits can make a chaotic iOS app accessible

links.author: Emma Camp (Reason)
key_points: Elite colleges report very high accommodation rates
Author blames social media and DSM changes
my_comments: Article questioning the rise in disability accommodations at elite colleges
links.summary: Opinion piece questioning very high disability-accommodation rates at elite universities (38% at Stanford), mostly for mental health and learning disabilities, attributing them to social media, looser diagnostic criteria and risk-averse affluent families. A contested viewpoint.
links.title: Why Are 38 Percent of Stanford Students Saying They're Disabled?

links.author: Ben Wintner (Fast Company)
key_points: Universal design often lacks emotional connection
my_comments: Discusses limitation of universal design, not about delighting the user
links.summary: Argues accessible design should go beyond compliance to how products make people feel, citing Michael Graves Design products that meet ADA standards while conveying dignity and pride.
links.title: The Next Revolution in Design: Emotional Accessibility

links.author: John Northup (WebAIM)
key_points: AI helps but humans judge quality
my_comments: WebAIM 2026 predictions
links.summary: WebAIM's seven predictions for 2026: AI speeds workflows but can't replace expert judgment, WCAG 2.2 becomes the procurement norm, native HTML over custom widgets, accessibility debt treated as business risk, web and native practice converging, respecting user preferences, and WCAG 3 thinking influencing practice early.
links.title: 2026 Predictions: The Next Big Shifts in Web Accessibility

links.author: Russ Weakley (Max Design)
key_points: DOM changes update the accessibility tree
my_comments: Nice explanation of how button works with JavaScript and browser
links.summary: Traces a click on an accordion button through hit-testing, JavaScript, DOM updates, accessibility-tree updates, OS accessibility APIs and the screen reader's speech queue, showing these happen concurrently rather than as a simple sequence.
links.title: What really happens when a user clicks an accordion button?

links.author: Access Aces
my_comments: Nice narrative about having a service dog at airport
links.title: Traveling with a Service Dog, Part 1

links.author: Katie McDermott (See Me Please)
key_points: ~75% of low-vision testers strongly preferred dark mode
my_comments: Dark mode
links.summary: Argues dark mode is an accessibility need, not a cosmetic preference, based on user testing where it was the most requested feature among low-vision, blind and neurodivergent testers. WCAG doesn't require it, and overlays or colour inversion are poor substitutes for native dark mode.
links.title: Dark Mode: Essential not a Preference

links.author: Eric Bailey (Piccalilli)
my_comments: How to make entire list cell clickable, but have clickable child elements
links.summary: Never nest interactive elements; instead use the 'semantic breakout' technique (a pseudo-element stretches the primary link over the card, with z-index keeping secondary actions clickable) to get the look of nested controls accessibly.
links.title: Accessible faux-nested interactive controls

links.author: Diogo Melo (Axess Lab)
key_points: Group product info into one element
Accessibility actions behave differently per AT
my_comments: Nice article about how to make an iOS app accessible to screen reader and keyboard users
links.summary: A blind iOS developer fixes a product list and wishlist for VoiceOver, Full Keyboard Access and Voice Control: star-rating labels, grouping product info, and accessibility actions for cart/wishlist, noting Voice Control needs directly exposed controls.
links.title: Making an iOS E-Commerce Product List Accessible to VoiceOver and Beyond

links.author: Diogo Melo (Axess Lab)
key_points: Combine elements + custom actions for VO
Each AT gets an optimized model
my_comments: Nice article on making iOS app accessible for VoiceOver without detrimentally affecting other assistive technologies
links.summary: Shows how to detect when VoiceOver is running (SwiftUI environment value or UIKit notifications) and switch to a combined, actions-based model for VoiceOver while leaving Full Keyboard Access and Voice Control with exposed controls.
links.title: Optimizing VoiceOver in an iOS E-Commerce App with Conditional Accessibility

links.author: Eric Bailey
key_points: APG demonstrates ARIA; it isn't a pattern library
Invest in your own semantic HTML docs
my_comments: How to be careful using APG for LLM
links.summary: Warns against feeding the whole ARIA Authoring Practices Guide to LLMs because its examples over-favor ARIA and vary in AT support. Recommends pointing LLMs only at pattern descriptions and keyboard-interaction sections, and prioritizing semantic HTML and your own design-system docs.
links.title: Here's how to instruct a LLM to reference the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide

links.author: Megan Dausch (Helen Keller National Center)
key_points: Concise labels matter on braille displays
Provide transcripts; test with braille users
my_comments: Nice article about braille users
links.summary: Braille display users read through a window of 12-80 cells, so verbose labels, unpredictable focus changes and fleeting dynamic content hit them hard. Self-voicing and audio-only interfaces exclude braille and DeafBlind users; include braille users in testing.
links.title: Between the Dots: What Designers Miss Without Braille Users

links.author: Blake Watson
key_points: Custom assistive tech built in ~8 hours
Free on GitHub, signed and notarized
Concerns about AI and developers' futures
my_comments: Vibe coding an ax feature
links.summary: A developer with spinal muscular atrophy used Claude Code with the GSD workflow to build 'Scroll My Mac', a macOS app for click-and-drag scrolling, in about 8 hours and roughly $80 of usage, and reflects on AI's promise and concerns for disabled makers.
links.title: I used Claude Code and GSD to build the accessibility tool I've always wanted

links.author: Russ Weakley (Max Design)
key_points: Can't cross shadow DOM; fails silently
my_comments: How aria-labelledby works under the hood
links.summary: Explains aria-labelledby: it names an element from existing on-page text by ID reference, outranks aria-label and native naming, can reference multiple IDs (including itself) and hidden content, fails silently on broken IDs, and can't cross shadow DOM.
links.title: How aria-labelledby really works

links.author: Russ Weakley (Max Design)
key_points: Typing echo is low priority and debounced
Screen reader output is filtered, not a log
my_comments: Nice explanation of how speech queues work for screen readers
links.summary: Uses a traffic-intersection analogy to explain why screen readers may or may not announce typed characters: typing echo is low priority and debounced, focus changes interrupt it, DOM batching merges changes, and some fields suppress echo.
links.title: More about screen reader speech queues

links.author: Manuel Matuzović
key_points: Popup must have the matching role
my_comments: Nice article explaining menu vs navigation
links.summary: aria-haspopup is often misused on navigation disclosure buttons. It declares a popup of a specific role (menu, listbox, tree, grid, dialog), and screen readers like JAWS then expect menu keyboard behavior. For site navigation, use aria-expanded instead.
links.title: aria-haspopup might not do what you think it does

links.author: Nat Tarnoff
my_comments: Nice explanation of how to address WCAG 2.5.1 with various options
links.summary: Explains WCAG 2.5.1 Pointer Gestures: multipoint or path-based gestures need single-pointer alternatives, and keyboard support should cover all mouse/touch interactions, e.g., buttons or arrow keys for drag-and-drop with live-region announcements.
links.title: A11y 101: 2.5.1 Pointer Gestures

links.author: Andrew Murphy
key_points: Faster output can make things worse
my_comments: Great article about issue with AI coding
links.summary: Argues AI coding tools speed up a step that usually isn't the bottleneck; real delays come from unclear requirements, review queues, deployment fear and organizational friction, so teams should map value streams and measure cycle time.
links.title: If you thought the speed of writing code was your problem - you have bigger problems

links.author: Dani Devesa Derksen-Staats (Accessibility up to 11)
my_comments: 365 tips for ios AX - like the format
links.summary: A year-long series of short daily iOS accessibility tips (230+ posts) on SwiftUI/UIKit accessibility modifiers, VoiceOver, Voice Control, Switch Control, Full Keyboard Access, Dynamic Type and testing.
links.title: #365DaysIOSAccessibility

links.author: Anna E. Cook
my_comments: AI perpetuating inaccessible products
links.summary: Argues AI can't fix accessibility; it relies on accessible, semantic, consistent systems to work at all. Cites WebAIM Million 2026 showing the first regression in six years, which she links to AI-assisted coding and budgets shifting from accessibility to AI.
links.title: AI Doesn't Fix Accessible Systems. It Depends on Them.

links.author: Dani Devesa Derksen-Staats (Accessibility up to 11)
my_comments: This author has experience with iOS AX
links.summary: How the author made RetroRapid!, an Apple Watch racing game, accessible: multiple inputs (Digital Crown, swipes, taps, keyboard), audio cues using musical notes, haptics, customizable settings, and non-stigmatizing difficulty names.
links.title: Learning to develop more accessible iOS games

links.author: Eric Bailey (GitHub Blog)
key_points: ~36% of WCAG criteria need manual evaluation
my_comments: AX agent developed by Github
links.summary: GitHub's pilot accessibility agent reviews pull requests and fixes simple issues; it has reviewed 3,535 PRs with a 68% resolution rate. Lessons: separate reviewer and implementer sub-agents, linear templated instructions, historical audit data, and escalation to humans.
links.title: Building a general-purpose accessibility agent, and what we learned in the process

links.author: Karol Wrótniak (Droids On Roids)
my_comments: Accessibility for cross-platform framework, Flutter
links.summary: Flutter accessibility techniques: ExcludeSemantics for decorative elements, BlockSemantics behind overlays, customSemanticsActions as gesture alternatives, and live regions for dynamic updates, compared with SwiftUI and Compose equivalents.
links.title: A Practical Guide to Flutter Accessibility Part 2: Hiding Noise, Exposing Actions

links.author: Hampus Sethfors (Axess Lab)
my_comments: Nice analysis of accessibility issues with an iOS app
links.summary: Axess Lab tested a conference site built with Lovable, which claimed 100% accessibility. A screen reader user found SPA focus problems, hidden menu/modal content being read, missing aria-expanded, skipped headings, label mismatches for voice control and a poorly marked language switcher.
links.title: Lovable's AI built a 100% accessible site – or did it?

links.author: AppleVis
links.status_note: Summary written from the homepage structure
links.summary: Community website for blind and low-vision users of Apple products, with app accessibility reviews and directory, guides, podcasts, forums and news about VoiceOver and iOS/macOS accessibility.
links.title: AppleVis

links.author: Rachele DiTullio
my_comments: Nice article on testing with different iOS settings, also has other related articles
links.title: 4 iOS display settings to check your app with

links.author: Adam Silver
my_comments: Article shows different interpretations of a WCAG criterion
links.summary: Argues against the accept attribute on file inputs: it greys out ineligible files without explanation, doesn't cover size limits or drag-and-drop, and hides errors rather than preventing them. Better to validate and show a clear error.
links.title: Why the accept attribute degrades file upload UX

links.author: GAAD Foundation with ServiceNow
my_comments: AI model comparison for accessibility
links.summary: Benchmark that asks 60 AI models to generate web pages in 28 categories and measures WCAG 2.2 AA violations with axe-core ('accessibility debt'). Results vary widely by provider and version; price doesn't predict accessibility; colour contrast dominates failures.
links.title: AIMAC: AI Model Accessibility Checker leaderboard

links.author: Karl Groves (AFixt)
key_points: Search engines model one non-interactive user
my_comments: SEO vs accessibility
links.summary: Analysis of 20 audits and 100,000+ automated failures finds only a small fraction of accessibility checks relate to SEO. The most common failures (dynamic content, ARIA, contrast, keyboard) are invisible to search engines, and some SEO tactics conflict with accessibility.
links.title: SEO is not accessibility, and we have the data to prove it

links.author: Ela Gorla (TetraLogical)
my_comments: Comprehensive article on how to design for deaf people
links.summary: Design considerations for D/deaf people beyond captions: accurate synced captions and transcripts, customizable captions, plain language, predefined form options, sign language for core content, and multiple contact methods instead of phone-only.
links.title: Designing for people who are D/deaf

links.author: Nathan Ortiz (Intopia)
key_points: Don't use empty elements for layout
my_comments: Nice article about how to handle when data is missing
links.summary: Five patterns for null or missing data in data-driven UIs so screen reader users don't meet empty elements and keyboard users don't land on dead controls: check data before rendering, don't style with empty elements, set defaults, use meaningful fallbacks, and put spacing on containers.
links.title: Handling Missing Data Without Breaking Accessibility

links.author: Anna E. Cook
my_comments: Insight about how discourse around AI is coercion, not invitation
Also mentions limitations of AI design prototyping for accessibility
links.summary: A satirical essay pushing back on 'adapt or perish' AI design-tool rhetoric: design needs thinking, collaboration and accountability; AI optimizes visual output while hiding structural and accessibility gaps.
links.title: Designing with Mustard

links.author: Grace Snow (TetraLogical)
my_comments: Nice article on how to design for reading disabilities
links.summary: Practical guidance for reducing reading effort: plain language and short sentences, left-aligned text at 70-80 characters, clear headings, legible fonts, a reading age around 9-11, expanded acronyms, and supporting visuals or audio.
links.title: Designing for people with reading disabilities

links.author: Mobile A11y
my_comments: iOS article about text - might be worth reading again
links.summary: Ten practical Dynamic Type tips: put text in scroll views, don't scale fixed bars, remove fixed heights, switch horizontal layouts to vertical at accessibility sizes, use line limits wisely, SF Symbols, @ScaledMetric, and test Bold Text and Display Zoom.
links.title: 10 Tips for Building iOS Apps That Handle Dynamic Type Well

links.author: Pedal Point
my_comments: Nice article on writing good alt text
links.title: Here's a simple recipe for good image alt text

links.author: A11yjobs
my_comments: Main job board for ax
links.summary: Job board for digital accessibility and assistive technology roles (consultants, engineers and more; remote, hybrid and on-site), plus newsletters, glossary, certifications and events.
links.title: A11yjobs

links.author: Access * Ability newsletter
key_points: Use spacing tools, not blank lines
my_comments: Insightful article about blanks
links.summary: Blank space is ambiguous to screen reader users, who can't tell intentional emptiness from a loading failure. Use explicit text (e.g., 'None' in table cells), proper paragraph spacing instead of blank lines, and announced empty states.
links.title: The Problem with Blanks for People Who Are Blind or Low Vision

links.author: Kat Homan (Smashing Magazine)
my_comments: Nice article on mental health considerations
links.summary: With ~95% of mental health app users gone by day 30, argues trendy UI patterns add cognitive friction, emotional mismatch and inconsistency for distressed users; offers a five-point framework for judging trends.
links.title: Designing For Distressed Users: Why Mental Health Apps Shouldn't Follow Every UI Fashion

links.author: Pluto Rennie (Salient)
key_points: Pressure to appear consistent and credible
my_comments: Interesting article about how you have to act a certain way when disabled
links.summary: Essay on the pressure for disabled people to present disability consistently and non-disruptively to be believed, while real bodies fluctuate; critiques care as a scarce, productivity-audited resource.
links.title: The Perfect Cripple: A User Guide to Being Palatable

links.author: Peter Torres Fremlin (Disability Debrief)
key_points: Aging brings disability to most people
my_comments: Overlap between ageism and disability, argues that we shouldn’t judge based on age
links.summary: Interview with anti-ageism activist Ashton Applewhite on how ageism and ableism intertwine, why older disabled people often resist disability identity, and adaptation and interdependence as shared human experiences.
links.title: Oh, it's happening to me

links.author: Nick Bevers (Spatie)
key_points: rem media queries follow the browser font setting
my_comments: Nice article that explains rem and how that works with page zoom
links.summary: Tailwind's rem-based breakpoints respond to users' browser font-size settings, which exceeds WCAG minimums, but can surprise developers who test at default size. Teams should choose deliberately between honoring font preferences and layout predictability.
links.title: Can we make default tailwind a more accessible choice?

links.author: Ken Nakata (Converge Accessibility)
key_points: Standing requires specific intent to return
Georgia and Utah anti-abuse statutes in effect
my_comments: Judge ruled that need intent to return to a website in order to be a valid accessibility lawsuit - used to dismiss cases where the plaintiff shows no intent to return
In “Bill Tracker” also has list of bills and their status
links.summary: Monthly US legal roundup: a Seventh Circuit standing dismissal (plaintiffs must allege specific intent to return), conflicting experts in a California case, a class certification with individualized Unruh claims, and state anti-abusive-litigation laws (Georgia HB 1470, Utah SB 68) and California bills.
links.title: Accessibility Legal Update July 2026

links.author: Graeme Coleman (TetraLogical)
key_points: iOS gets it by default in SwiftUI
my_comments: Nice article on native accessibility
Claims iOS supports heading levels
links.summary: Argues native app screen titles should be exposed as headings (like an h1) under WCAG 1.3.1. Testing popular apps found iOS apps did this (SwiftUI's default) while most Android apps did not; Compose makes it easier than XML Views.
links.title: Should native app screen titles be headings?

links.author: T-Mobile Accessibility Resource Center
my_comments: Has native app accessibility criteria
links.summary: Open-source tool from T-Mobile that generates accessibility acceptance criteria and test instructions for web and native components, so product teams can build and verify accessible experiences.
links.title: MagentaA11y

links.author: unattributed.cc
my_comments: Reader mode in browsers - learned something new!
links.title: Accessibility rant: reader mode

links.author: T-Mobile Accessibility Resource Center
my_comments: Has nice advice on how to handle alt text for charts
links.status_note: Section of the MagentaA11y tool (entry 112); page needs JavaScript so summary is based on the tool's structure
links.summary: MagentaA11y's testing criteria for images: acceptance criteria and step-by-step manual test instructions (keyboard, screen reader) for informative and decorative images.
links.title: MagentaA11y: how to test images

links.author: Appt Foundation
key_points: WCAG applies to apps as well as web
my_comments: Each WCAG criteria has tips for how to implement on Android and iOS
links.summary: Appt's overview of WCAG 2.2 for apps: 4 principles, 13 guidelines, 87 success criteria across levels A/AA/AAA, how they apply to mobile apps, and links to EN 301 549 and Section 508.
links.title: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) | Appt

links.author: Deborah de Quevedo (The Doctors Company)
my_comments: AX medical regulation for disability - notice that some deadlines in 2027 and 2028
links.summary: Explains the May 2024 HHS Section 504 rule for healthcare providers receiving federal funds: accessible exam tables and scales, and WCAG 2.1 AA for websites, apps and kiosks, with deadlines in 2026-2028.
links.title: HHS Accessibility Rule: Fast-Approaching Compliance Deadlines for Healthcare Providers

links.author: Open Source Guides (GitHub)
key_points: Add to PR checklists and templates
my_comments: Open Source ax tips
links.summary: How to make open source projects accessible: partner with disabled people, publish an accessibility statement, accessible docs, keyboard-friendly native UI, automated plus manual testing, and accessibility in PR checklists and issue templates.
links.title: Accessibility Best Practices for Your Project

links.author: WebAIM
my_comments: Comprehensive checklist for WCAG criteria
links.summary: Simplified, practical checklist of WCAG 2.2 success criteria organized by principle, filterable by WCAG version and level, with links to W3C specs and WebAIM techniques.
links.title: WebAIM's WCAG 2 Checklist

links.author: David Bushell
my_comments: Explains why should be careful when using APG, it purposely over-indexes on using ARIA
links.title: ARIA anti-patterns and you

links.author: Sightless Scribbles
my_comments: Shows how prototyping practices in Silicon Valley can lead to inaccessible products
links.title: Disability dongle

links.author: W3C
key_points: Most criteria apply to non-web ICT
my_comments: WCAG interpretation for non-web applications
links.summary: W3C note on applying WCAG 2.0/2.1/2.2 success criteria to non-web documents and software, replacing 'web page' with 'document' or 'software' and addressing closed-functionality systems.
links.title: Guidance on Applying WCAG 2 to Non-Web ICT (WCAG2ICT)

links.author: Dave Gunn (DAISY Consortium)
my_comments: DAISY format
How making e-books accessible
links.summary: South Korea's National Library for the Disabled uses AI: an online EPUB verification system with a chatbot to help publishers produce born-accessible books, and generative AI trials to speed accessible-format production, with human oversight.
links.title: Smart Libraries: AI Use in South Korea

links.author: Adrian Roselli
my_comments: Considerations for dialogs
links.summary: Depends on context: action-required dialogs (legal, warnings, logins) shouldn't close on outside click; informational ones can; sheets and drawers need judgment about data loss, visibility of the page underneath and recovery.
links.title: Should a Dialog Close When Clicked Outside?

links.author: Nic Steenhout
key_points: Accessibility lacks an owner at handoffs
my_comments: Describes case of AX considered in design but then wasn’t implemented with AX
links.summary: Why accessible designs become inaccessible products: workflow gaps rather than individual failures. Handoffs lack ownership, design reviews don't document implementation, and end-of-project audits come too late. Add checkpoints throughout.
links.title: Accessibility getting dropped in the process

links.author: The A11Y Project
my_comments: WCAG checklist
links.summary: Beginner-friendly WCAG-based checklist in 18 categories (content, global code, keyboard, images, headings, forms, media and more), each item linked to its success criterion.
links.title: Checklist - The A11Y Project

links.author: AAArdvark
my_comments: Goes into WCAG in detail
links.summary: Plain-language explanation of WCAG criteria, browsable by principle, guideline, theme, level, disability type and responsibility (code, content, design). Not a replacement for official WCAG.
links.title: WCAG in Plain English

links.author: Jeff Adams (UsableNet)
my_comments: Article on limitations of AI to build accessible sites
links.summary: AI can generate storefronts quickly but reproduces inaccessible patterns from its training data. Automated scans cover only about 25-30% of requirements, iterative AI changes can quietly regress accessibility, and expert oversight plus AT user testing remain essential.
links.title: AI and Accessibility for Ecommerce: What the Tools Really Do and What they Don't

links.author: CVS Health
links.summary: Open-source Android sample app with 29 accessibility techniques for View-based UIs (basics, grouping and ordering, dynamic behavior, specific components), each documented, plus Espresso accessibility testing examples.
links.title: android-view-accessibility-techniques

links.author: CVS Health
links.summary: Open-source sample app with 30+ documented accessibility techniques for Jetpack Compose (informative content, interactive behaviors, specific components) in Kotlin.
links.title: android-compose-accessibility-techniques

links.author: W3C
key_points: Many questions answered by WG members
my_comments: Good resource if unsure whether is a WCAG failure
Issues tab is also good for this
links.summary: The W3C WCAG repository's GitHub Discussions forum, where practitioners ask clarification questions about WCAG 2.2 and WCAG 3 success criteria (focus visibility, contrast, reflow, labels, pointer gestures) and get answers from the community and working group members.
links.title: W3C WCAG GitHub Discussions

links.author: TetraLogical
my_comments: Another major AX company
links.summary: UK accessibility consultancy offering audits, consultancy, training and strategy, with a team of screen reader and ARIA specialists, and a widely read blog and free newsletter series.
links.title: TetraLogical

links.author: Cam Coulter
my_comments: Cam Coulter’s presentation about WCAG, has a bunch of great resources in it
links.summary: Presentation notes on a structured way to learn WCAG: understand its structure (principles, guidelines, success criteria), learn HTML/CSS/JS and ARIA, practice testing with tools and screen readers, and join the community.
links.title: How to Learn WCAG

links.author: Sheri Byrne-Haber
key_points: Contrast is only part of the story
Offer both light and dark modes
my_comments: In-depth article about limitations of WCAG criteria for color
links.summary: WCAG's colour criteria cover only a fraction of colour accessibility. Discusses colour vision deficiency, sensory sensitivity to saturated colours, migraine/photophobia triggers, seizure risk from static striped patterns, and the need for both light and dark themes.
links.title: Accessible Color Choices Are About So Much More Than Just Contrast

links.author: Russ Weakley (Max Design)
my_comments: Aria-details property and how differs from aria-describedby
links.summary: aria-details points to extended, structured information without having screen readers read it all automatically, letting users choose to explore it. Contrasts it with aria-describedby, which is read as part of the element's description and suits short text.
links.title: Understanding aria-details

links.author: Patrick H. Lauke (YouTube)
my_comments: Patrick Lauke’s presentation on how to interpret WCAG
links.title: Patrick Lauke: how to interpret WCAG (presentation)

links.author: Ricky Onsman
key_points: AI complements, not replaces, professional judgment
Audits carry an evidentiary burden, so findings must be evidence-based
Biggest value: broader thinking, more disability perspectives, edge cases, consistency, less admin
Testing with disabled people remains essential
my_comments: I really like this sentence "The highest value lies in helping expert auditors think more broadly, cover more disability perspectives, explore edge cases, improve consistency, and reduce the administrative burden of auditing."
links.summary: How accessibility auditors can use AI as a supporting 'junior partner' while keeping testing evidence-based. AI can review large amounts of content quickly, but its output needs expert review, auditors stay accountable for conclusions, and usability testing with disabled people can't be reliably simulated.
links.title: Using AI as Your Accessibility Testing Partner

links.author: Adrian Roselli
my_comments: It gives really good tips on how to evaluate a WCAG criterion.
links.status_note: Site rate-limited automated reading on 2026-09-24; summary to be added later
links.title: Evaluating a Success Criterion

links.author: Michele A. Williams (Accessibility Talks)
my_comments: "If exclusion is the norm, access will always feel exceptional"
links.status_note: YouTube blocked automated reading; summary to be added later
links.title: Exclusion by Design - Michele A. Williams

links.author: Appt Foundation
links.summary: Overview of the main assistive technologies used with apps (screen readers, voice control, switch control, keyboard access) with links to Android and iOS documentation for each.
links.title: Assistive technologies for using apps

links.author: Appt Foundation (research by Q42)
key_points: Font size and dark mode most common
links.summary: Anonymous data from millions of Dutch iOS and Android users: over half have at least one accessibility setting on (about 50% of iOS users, nearly 75% of Android). Visual settings like dark mode and font size are most common.
links.title: Accessibility Stats

links.author: World Health Organization
key_points: Twice the risk of depression, diabetes and more
links.summary: An estimated 1.3 billion people (about 16%, 1 in 6) have significant disability. They face health inequities, earlier death and higher risk of chronic conditions due to stigma, poverty and inaccessible health systems.
links.title: Disability and health (fact sheet)

links.author: Appt Foundation
links.my_label: Appt.org guide for making ax apps
links.summary: Nonprofit knowledge base for accessible mobile apps: usage statistics, code documentation for iOS, Android, React Native, Flutter and Xamarin, WCAG guidance for apps, articles and a free handbook.
links.title: Appt.org: A guide for making apps accessible

links.author: Google
key_points: Accessibility section for Views and Compose
links.status_note: Summary written from general knowledge of the site
links.summary: Google's official Android developer site, including the accessibility guides for making apps work with TalkBack, Switch Access, Voice Access and large text in both Views and Jetpack Compose.
links.title: Android Developers

links.author: Apple
links.status_note: Summary written from general knowledge of the site
links.summary: Apple's official developer site, including Human Interface Guidelines and accessibility documentation for VoiceOver, Dynamic Type, Voice Control and Switch Control in SwiftUI and UIKit.
links.title: Apple Developer

links.author: Appt Foundation
links.my_label: Appt.org native vs cross platform frameworks
links.summary: Compares accessibility API support in native Android/iOS vs Flutter, React Native and Xamarin: native and Flutter have full support, React Native about 90% (e.g., no focus order control), Xamarin 50-80%.
links.title: Native versus cross-platform frameworks to develop accessible apps

links.author: Abra
links.my_label: Abra differences between native, web, and hybrid apps
links.summary: Explains native, cross-platform and hybrid (webview) apps and how framework choice affects accessibility capability and compliance; recommends testing accessibility early.
links.title: Key Differences Between Native, Web, and Hybrid Apps

links.author: Council of the European Union
links.summary: About 90 million Europeans (24% of adults) have a disability, rising steeply with age (47% over 65). Disabled people face higher discrimination, unemployment and poverty risk.
links.title: Disability in the EU: facts and figures

links.author: Jan Jaap de Groot and Paul van Workum (Appt)
links.summary: Free app accessibility handbook (2nd edition, English and Dutch) covering the basics in plain language and updated for WCAG 2.2; PDF download or printed copy.
links.title: Appt Accessibility Handbook

links.author: Appt Foundation
key_points: ~19.5% of Dutch people have age-related impairments
links.summary: Overview of six groups of disabilities that affect app use (cognitive, hearing, mobility, speech, visual, and age-related), with Dutch prevalence figures, and a reminder that disabilities can be permanent, temporary or situational.
links.title: Disabilities when using apps

links.author: Appt Foundation
key_points: Enable via Settings, Siri or shortcut
links.summary: How to turn on and use VoiceOver on iOS: activation options, core gestures (swipe to move, double-tap to activate), multi-finger gestures, the rotor, and settings like speech rate.
links.title: VoiceOver: screen reader for iOS

links.author: Appt Foundation

links.summary: Setup and command reference for Android Voice Access: enabling it, numbered labels and grid overlays, and voice commands for navigation, gestures, text editing and settings.

key_points: iOS Switch Control / Android Switch Access

key_points: Easier than touch for some motor disabilities

links.author: Abra
links.summary: EN 301 549 v4.1.0 aligns the EU standard with WCAG 2.2: web views in apps are treated as non-web software (Clause 11), four new criteria (focus, dragging, target size, authentication) are added, and some previously void criteria now apply to apps.
links.title: Mobile App Accessibility under EN 301 549 v4.1.0

links.author: W3C WAI
links.summary: Catalog of Accessibility Conformance Testing (ACT) rules for WCAG 2.2 and ARIA, which standardize how to test specific requirements; filterable by requirement, status and implementation (manual, automated, linters).

key_points: Covers all WCAG 2.2 A/AA criteria for mobile
links.summary: W3C draft note on applying WCAG 2.2 A and AA success criteria to native, mobile web and hybrid apps, replacing web terms (e.g., 'web page') with mobile concepts like screens and views. Informative, not normative.
